newsitem.title: USA: Weather drives oil, grain markets higher.
newsitem.headline: Weather drives oil, grain markets higher.

text.p: Forecasts for wintry weather in the Northeast pushed energy prices higher Monday as rumors of weather-related damage to wheat and corn crops sparked a similar rally in grain prices.
Gold fell to its lowest level in more than three years as investors shunned the metal and turned to the stock markets.
The Knight-Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures rose 1.81 to close at 242.09 points.
Weather forecasters said the Northeast, the largest heating oil market in the world, will experience temperatures greatly below normal by late this week and that the cold would last into next week.
Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis in Chicago said temperatures could drop 10 to 20 degrees below normal in the eastern third of the nation from Friday to Monday.
The forecasts, plus a return to freezing temperatures in the Midwest, sent heating fuel prices soaring.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, heating oil for February delivery closed up a sharp 2.35 cents a gallon at 73.64 cents.
Natural gas futures jumped 17 percent, with February contracts ending up 53 cents to close at $3.636 per million British thermal units.
Buoyed by those gains, gasoline and crude oil also rose.
February gasoline finished up 1.82 cents at 72.52 cents a gallon. February crude rose 78 cents a barrel to $26.37.
"There is cold weather across a broad portion of the United States, so things should stay pretty firm," said Sweeney Oil trader Jim Ritterbusch.
Crude was helped in part by news of tightening supply.
With the post-Gulf War high of $26.80 hit Dec. 19 close at hand, Texaco said the amount of crude it was to buy from Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organization has been reduced at Iraq's request.

Iraq reduced the amount of crude it will export, citing worries that high oil prices might mean it would overshoot the sales limit of $1 billion of oil over three months under its "oil-for-food" deal with the United Nations.
New York precious metals prices ended sharply lower for the fourth session in a row, with spot gold prices down more than $10 an ounce, or 2.8 percent, in the first three trading days of the year.
February gold on the New York Mercantile Exchange's COMEX division closed down $3.30 an ounce at $358.70, after seeing a new life-of-contract low at $357.60.
The last time gold traded at current levels was in early October 1993, when it hovered at $350.00.

"This is the first week of the new year and we're at three-year lows," said Ted Arnold, an analyst at Merrill Lynch in London. "Increasingly it looks like the downside is wide open. In 1997, I think $330 looks possible."
March silver ended down 3.3 cents at $4.652 an ounce.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn and wheat prices shot higher.

March wheat gained 4-1/2 cents a bushel to close at $3.88-1/2. Traders were concerned about recent unseasonably warm weather in the winter wheat fields of the Plains states melting the crop's protective snow cover and making the plants more vulnerable to "winter kill" from a sudden freeze.
March corn rose 1/2 cent a bushel to $2.57 as talk swept the market that southern Argentina needed more rain for its corn and soybean crops.
January soybeans closed at $6.94 a bushel, down 2-1/4 cents, after rising as high as $7.05 earlier in the day.
